key_gap: Both sides produced the same skeleton — dependency-ordered chunks (plan literacy → index design → stats/join order → integrated tuning), per-chunk mastery bars, interleaved retrieval, and a Friday mentor gate — and both fit the 60-hour envelope, but the human's two decisively gradeable elements were first-class while the AI's were afterthoughts: (1) the edge rule — the human specifies a measured 70–85% solve-rate band with explicit raise/lower triggers driven by per-chunk mastery bars ('the bar says which chunk to push, the band says how hard'), while the AI's difficulty rule stayed verbal ('challenging but solvable') until its REVIEW stage admitted the deficit; (2) the plateau detector — the human designs a trigger metric into the schedule from week 4 (<15% weekly gain for 2 weeks → re-diagnose the failing chunk, drop difficulty, change material, escalate to mentor), while the AI treated plateau handling as a contingency note assembled after the plan was complete. On skill-acquisition plans, measurement is the product: a plan whose edge and plateau controls are not numeric will degrade to ritual at exactly the documented week-3–5 stall.
learning_signal: Skill-acquisition plan quality lives in measurement, not structure: chunk decomposition earns nothing unless each chunk carries a measurable mastery bar, and the edge-of-ability rule must be a numeric success band (e.g., 70–85% weekly solve rate) with explicit difficulty-adjustment logic — verbal bands are not gradeable and reproduce ritual practice. Design the plateau detector into the schedule up front (a trigger metric like <15% weekly gain for 2 weeks, with named responses: re-diagnose which chunk's bar fails, lower difficulty, change material, escalate to a coach), never as a post-hoc contingency. Wire the two together: mastery bars determine which chunk to push; the band determines how hard. Schedule spacing and interleaved retrieval of mastered chunks on a fixed cadence, and give every week a pass/fail gate tied to a bar.
suggested_improvement: Add a 'practice-plan quality gate' to the HOW stage for skill-acquisition tasks: (a) require a numeric edge band (success-rate range + raise/lower triggers) before any schedule is accepted; (b) require a designed-in plateau detector with a named trigger metric and per-contingency actions, present in the plan from the first draft, not added at REVIEW; (c) require every chunk to carry a measurable mastery bar and state explicitly how the bar feeds the difficulty rule; (d) run the verification pass against the 'ritual test' — if removing the numbers would leave the plan functionally unchanged, the plan is still a syllabus; (e) in REVIEW, check that any element flagged as underspecified in the first draft (as difficulty was here) gets closed before the decision packet, not listed as a future refinement.

key_gap: The pure style reproduced its registry weakness — feedback-dependent + plateau-focused — at full fidelity: it framed the incident loop as a skill plateau, chunked debugging skill (log triage → hypothesis → verification → fix), designed edge drills in a 70–85% band, and even built a plateau breaker, but it never audited the feedback channel and never looked outside practice. It treated the truncated log excerpts as drill fidelity ('real incidents truncate, so drills should too') when truncation was the reason the team mis-diagnosed the same root cause twice, and it accepted 'synthetic' drill incidents built from that mis-diagnosis — so the regime would have automated the wrong lesson, with 9/14 incidents' shared cross-shard design flaw untouched. The AI ran a feedback-validity audit in WHY before judging the plan: it asked whether the practice signal itself was true and complete, classified the plateau as a design/tooling ceiling (truncated statements, no telemetry, 45-min build), rejected the wholesale regime, and returned a hybrid — observability + design fix with metrics first, deliberate practice re-gated on a clean repro harness, with an explicit unlock condition so the manager could not read the verdict as anti-training. On any recurring-failure loop, the first question is not 'what to practice' but 'can the learner see the failure'.
learning_signal: Before prescribing practice for any plateau, audit the feedback channel: is the practice signal true and complete? Truncated logs, missing telemetry, and slow builds corrupt the feedback that deliberate practice depends on — drills built on a mis-diagnosed root cause automate the wrong lesson. Distinguish a skill plateau (practice fixes it) from a design/tooling ceiling (evidence: recurring incidents sharing one root cause that was mis-diagnosed precisely because the evidence was truncated; accurate post-mortems whenever the evidence is visible). When the channel is broken, the fix is tooling-first with named metrics (full statement capture, lock-wait/query-timing telemetry, fast CI, deterministic repro harness), then the structural fix, and deliberate practice is deferred — not banned — and re-gated on the clean harness, with an explicit unlock condition and re-check date.
suggested_improvement: Add a 'feedback-validity audit' to the WHY stage for any plateau/recurring-failure diagnosis: (a) before evaluating any practice plan, check the feedback channel — can the team see the failing artifact complete? is the iteration loop fast enough? are the practice materials built on verified root causes?; (b) run an explicit plateau-vs-ceiling test: does the evidence support a skill deficit (post-mortems accurate when evidence is visible), and do the incidents share a design generator that practice cannot touch?; (c) if the channel is corrupt, route to a tooling/design-first alternative with named metrics and a 4-week re-check, and re-gate any training regime on the clean harness with a stated unlock condition; (d) guard the recommendation's reception — explicitly say the regime is deferred, not cancelled, so the verdict cannot be read as anti-training; (e) in REVIEW, log the drift pull ('the lead believes in practice because it built her skill') as a named bias and verify the selected plan against the incident generator, not against training doctrine.
